claimGate.detail: ct-destruction-request and ct-provisional-pardon are recorded on VF20, released 2026-09-09T11:48:43.129Z and ...227Z respectively. ct-absolute-pardon is recorded on VF05, released 2026-09-09T11:48:42.386Z. assessmentValidation.command: assessConnecticutReviewedGuidance(root, familyId) from scripts/grade-a-packet-factory-24h/ct-reviewed-guidance.mjs, run in this worktree at HEAD
assessmentValidation.note: The assessment already returns eligible:true for all three families and did so before I touched anything. Eligibility was never the blocker.
assessmentValidation.gateProof: I then ran applyConnecticutGuidanceAcceptance with the real selected return and a maximally favourable context (readiness ready, nineZero true, no legal block, no delivery-type refusal, no source hold). It returned PRODUCT_PATH_PENDING for all three - held solely because closedCurrentVerdicts is empty and the selected identity is not priorSelectedReturn. In a read-only in-memory counterfactual that added a correctly shaped closure carrying the verdictSha256 values recorded above, the same call returned GUIDANCE_READY for all three. That confirms the digests I computed are the exact ones the gate compares against, and that the only missing thing is a closure I decline to write. Nothing was written to disk by that experiment.

whereClosureEntriesWouldHaveToLive.answer: Inside SESSION10_CT_GUIDANCE_ROWS.json itself. A separate successor record is not an option without a code change.
whereClosureEntriesWouldHaveToLive.readFromCode: CT_GUIDANCE_REVIEW is a hardcoded constant at ct-reviewed-guidance.mjs line 8. assessConnecticutReviewedGuidance reads that one path (line 120), selects the family row from review.families (line 134), and takes closedCurrentVerdicts from row.closedCurrentVerdicts and nowhere else (lines 159, 170, 188). I grepped the whole scripts and src trees: the only other reader is the test harness. There is no override for the review path and no successor path is consulted.
whereClosureEntriesWouldHaveToLive.inertSuccessorKeys: SESSION10_CT_GUIDANCE_ROWS.json carries top-level sourceOnlySuccessor and provisionalCurrentDeltaSuccessor blocks that look like successor plumbing. They are inert: grep finds no code that reads either key. They are documentation of how the review itself was layered, not a channel the checker follows.
whereClosureEntriesWouldHaveToLive.doesEditingItBreakItsOwnPin: No - and this is worth stating precisely so nobody avoids the edit for the wrong reason. The review is not pinned to a constant digest. reviewSha256 is computed from the bytes read (line 185). The two publication assertions (lines 127-128) compare the file against itself at HEAD and at `git log -1 -- <that path>`, both of which recompute after any commit touching it. So a commit that edits the review satisfies both assertions by construction. The real objection to editing it is authorship, not hashing: it is another lane’s review record, and a third lane writing findings into it would misattribute them to the session10 reviewer.
whereClosureEntriesWouldHaveToLive.recommendation: If the Captain ever wants current-verdict closure to be possible without one lane writing into another lane’s review record, the fix is a code change to ct-reviewed-guidance.mjs adding an explicit successor-record path with its own attribution and its own publication assertions - not a data edit. No such change is needed for this dispatch, because I am closing nothing.
